source.title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
source.authors: Shaowen Wang; Ge Zhang; Kai-Rong Luo; Yu-Hao Wu; Shao-Fan Liu; Jia-Heng Liu; Wen-Hao Huang; Shen Yan; Jian Li

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to compute-matched MoE looped Transformers, fitting held-out loss surfaces and examining compute-optimal allocations and downstream outcomes.
record.gate_note: The paper fits loss-scaling surfaces to its own held-out validation-loss results and reports compute-frontier and downstream-residual results. It cites earlier scaling studies and their findings, but those cited results are not rows. The loop-design ablations are used to choose the recipe; they are not recorded as scaling-law results.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla Approach-3 loss surfaces to its own held-out validation losses for sparse MoE models, plain and looped, from 1.3e19 to 2.2e21 FLOPs. It derives compute-optimal splits and calibrates downstream scores against validation loss. This is a new setting (MoE, a per-token-FLOPs capacity axis, looping) with its own results on V1, V4, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that looping the middle half twice beats a budget-matched MoE Baseline at all scales and sparsities. Its fitted frontier falls faster and saves 6.8–18.0% compute at 1e20–1e21 FLOPs with nearly the same optimal split. Downstream gains exceed what validation loss predicts, concentrate on code, long samples and in-context examples, and are tied mechanistically to a reduced attention sink on the second visit.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Chinchilla-style loss-scaling method, adapted for MoE by using measured per-token FLOPs and compute-equivalent sparsity rather than a single parameter-count axis. Separate surfaces are fit for Baseline and SMELT.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper excludes S=0 dense-reference endpoints because including them worsens sparse-grid surface RMSE. It states that compute-optimal conclusions are sensitive to fitting choices, but does not report a systematic variation of its own fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: A looped MoE architecture has a steeper fitted compute-frontier exponent (γ 0.250 vs 0.237) and saves 6.8–18% compute at equal loss within the fitted range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural changes can alter scaling-frontier exponents, not just offsets, under matched FLOPs, parameters and KV cache.

record.problems: The full architecture and training stack are proprietary, and pretraining uses an internal corpus. Each configuration is trained once, so reported evaluation-seed errors do not capture training-run variability. The scaling fit excludes the dense-reference regime and supports compute predictions only within its stated range; larger-budget behavior is not anchored by runs.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-law rows were omitted. The loop-span, depth, and loop-count ablations in Tables 3–5 are recipe-selection results rather than direct tests of the listed scaling-law versions, so they are not included.

untested.parts: Parameter-count axis (capacity is per-token FLOPs); the dense S=0 regime; behaviour beyond 2.2e21 FLOPs.
Entirely. The 1e22 values in Table 7 are flagged as extrapolated and never checked against runs.
Entirely, as an empirical claim. Allocations are power laws by construction of the fit and are reported at one budget only.
No systematic variation of fitting method, schedule or parameter counting.

missing.what: Baseline depth sweep at fixed FLOPs, parameters and KV cache: loss 1.9638/1.9445/1.9457/1.9542 for L=9/12/15/18
Baseline loss-to-benchmark sigmoid calibration quality (R² 0.997, 0.974, 0.911 on 96 endpoints)
S=0 dense-reference endpoints excluded because a joint fit with the sparse grid worsens RMSE (single surface does not span both regimes)

record.verdict_notes: R3–R5 were relinked to none because they compare the study's method with its Baseline. V3 is not empirically tested: the power-law allocation is implied by the fit form at a single budget. The derived exponent F*∝C^(c/(a+c))≈0.64 is Kaplan-like, but the paper does not state it. The Table 4 depth sweep was wrongly left out as recipe selection; it bears on V4.

versions.untested_parts: No direct parameter-count-only scaling fit is reported; the fitted capacity axis is measured per-token FLOPs, with compute-equivalent sparsity as an additional variable. The dense-reference S=0% regime is excluded from the scaling-law fit.

The paper fits across its full sparse grid rather than testing predictions from small runs against held-out larger runs. It says runs at larger budgets would be needed to anchor predictions beyond the fitted range.
The paper derives power-law allocation formulas from its fitted surfaces and reports allocations at C = 10^21, but does not empirically test the allocation trend across multiple compute budgets.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count aimed at testing whether loss changes only slightly.
The study concerns text pretraining and does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
Downstream predictability is assessed for DCLM Completion, DCLM Core, and MMLU using a calibration against validation loss; other downstream tasks or general predictive laws are not tested.

The paper compares fitted exponents for two architectures under one shared fitting protocol. It does not vary parameter-counting conventions, data, schedule, or fitting method systematically, and does not test whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Baseline
rows.size_stated: 100M, 200M, 600M, and 1.6B active non-embedding parameter scales; total non-embedding parameter range 0.1B–53.89B
rows.operation_detail: Fit the Chinchilla-style held-out loss surface L(F,S,D) separately for the Baseline.
rows.measure: Fitted loss-surface coefficients (E, A, K, a, b, c) and RMSE
rows.note: The fitted form is L(F,S,D)=E+A(1−S)^b/F^a+K/D^c. The fit is over the sparse grid, not a direct parameter-count-only axis.
rows.check: The surface fits the Baseline's 72 sparse endpoints with RMSE 0.0055 nats; positive exponents a=0.370 and c=0.659. The capacity axis is per-token FLOPs, not parameters. Drop the V7 link: exponent differences between architectures are an architecture effect, not a setup or fitting choice.

rows.measure: Fitted loss-surface coefficients (E, A, K, a, b, c) and RMSE
rows.note: The same fitting procedure yields different capacity and data exponents for SMELT and the Baseline.
rows.check: The surface fits SMELT's 72 endpoints with RMSE 0.0095 nats; a=0.389, c=0.701. Drop the V7 link for the same reason as R1.

rows.subject: SMELT
rows.operation_detail: Compare downstream scores with a monotone sigmoid calibration fitted from 96 Baseline validation-loss endpoints.
rows.measure: Downstream residual beyond the score predicted from validation loss
rows.value: Residual is positive at every scale and increases monotonically with scale
rows.note: The authors report that SMELT outperforms the Baseline-fitted curve, so validation loss alone underpredicts its downstream gains.
rows.check: The loss-to-score calibration fitted on the Baseline under-predicts SMELT: residual is positive (≈+1.7 to +12 mn by scale, Fig 9a). The loss→downstream mapping is not architecture-invariant. The value could carry the Fig 9a numbers.
